prompt: What does the word "NoSQL" actually name?

choices.text: A family of databases that all store data without a schema
choices.why: The families differ on exactly this; MongoDB can validate a schema and Cassandra requires one.

choices.text: Every kind of database that is not relational
choices.why: Right. The products under the name have less in common with each other than with Postgres.

choices.text: A query language that replaces SQL across the products
choices.why: Each product has its own interface: mongosh, Redis commands, CQL.

choices.text: Databases designed to run on many machines
choices.why: Postgres can run on many machines too, and Redis is often a single server.

prompt: Redis and MongoDB can both hold order 1001 as one value under one name. What is the difference between them that the lesson asks you to watch?
hint: Two things to watch: the unit, and something about the unit.

choices.text: Whether the server can read inside the value to answer a query
choices.why: Right. MongoDB reads every field; Redis hands the value back whole and knows nothing of its contents.

choices.text: Whether the value is kept on disk or only in the server's memory
choices.why: Persistence matters (lesson 13), but it is not what decides which questions each can answer.

choices.text: Whether the whole order can be read back in a single request
choices.why: Both hand the whole order back in one request; that is what they share.

choices.text: Whether the value is stored as JSON text or in a binary format
choices.why: Redis held JSON text and still could not read a field of it; the format is not the point.

prompt: An analytics team will ask questions about the shop's orders that nobody can list today. Which property of a store matters most to them?

choices.text: How fast a value is returned when its key is already known
choices.why: That serves questions planned in advance, which is the opposite of their situation.

choices.text: How many rows a single partition can hold
choices.why: A partition answers questions about one key; unplanned questions cross partitions.

choices.text: That the server sees inside what it stores and joins it when read
choices.why: Right. Seeing inside and joining at read time is what answers a question nobody planned for.

choices.text: That every write is acknowledged by every copy of the data before it returns
choices.why: That is a consistency setting from lesson 1; it says nothing about which questions are possible.

prompt: In which family is reading order 1001 back a join assembled from several tables on every read?

choices.text: Wide column, because each order line is its own row
choices.why: The lines are rows, but all of them sit in Ana's partition and come back in one read.

choices.text: Relational
choices.why: Right. Each fact is stored once, and the order is rebuilt from orders, order_lines, customers and products.

choices.text: Graph
choices.why: A graph follows the links stored beside each node; it does not join tables.

choices.text: Document, because the customer lives elsewhere
choices.why: The order itself, lines included, came back from one document; the customer's city would be a second read, not a join.

prompt: Why does the lesson store `unit_price` as `Decimal128("39.90")` rather than as the number 39.90?

choices.text: Because MongoDB refuses numbers with a fractional part
choices.why: It accepts them, as binary floating-point doubles, which is the problem.

choices.text: Because a decimal type sorts faster in an index
choices.why: Speed is not the reason given; exactness is.

choices.text: Because 39.90 has no exact binary floating-point form
choices.why: Right. Decimal128 keeps decimal digits, so 268.80 is stored as typed.

choices.text: Because Redis and Cassandra need the same type to read it
choices.why: Each store keeps its own copy in its own types; none reads MongoDB's.

prompt: `findOne({ _id: 1001 })` returned the customer, the date, both lines and the total. Why was no join needed?

choices.text: Because mongosh joins collections on the client, out of sight
choices.why: There was only one collection involved; nothing was joined anywhere.

choices.text: Because the lines were written inside the order
choices.why: Right. The unit stored is the unit read: one document, one lookup.

choices.text: Because `_id` is indexed and the index stores the whole document
choices.why: The index finds the document; it is the document that holds the lines.

choices.text: Because MongoDB has no way to relate two collections
choices.why: It has one, `$lookup`, in lesson 8; it was simply not needed here.

prompt: The `orders` collection grows to two million documents with no index besides `_id`. What does `find({ "lines.sku": "MS-204" })` do?
hint: Seeing inside is not the same as being fast inside.

choices.text: It is refused until an index on `lines.sku` exists
choices.why: MongoDB runs it; refusing a scan is Cassandra's habit, not MongoDB's.

choices.text: It reads every document and returns the matching ones
choices.why: Right. The answer is correct and the cost grows with the collection, until lesson 7's index.

choices.text: It looks only at the first line of each order, since arrays are not searched
choices.why: The query matched order 1001 by its second line, the mouse.

choices.text: It returns an error, because nested fields need `$lookup`
choices.why: Dot notation reaches nested fields directly; `$lookup` joins collections.

prompt: Ana ordered at 10:22 in São Paulo, and `findOne` showed `13:22:00.000Z`, because MongoDB stores dates in ___.
hint: The Z at the end names it.

prompt: Order 1001 is stored with `SET` as JSON text. Why does `HGET order:1001 total` answer `WRONGTYPE`?

choices.text: Because the field is called `total` in the JSON but `TOTAL` in Redis's own hash
choices.why: No field exists at all; to Redis the value is one string.

choices.text: Because `HGET` only reads keys created in the same session
choices.why: Keys do not belong to sessions.

choices.text: Because JSON has to be stored with a JSON-specific command
choices.why: Plain Redis has no JSON type; the lesson's point is that the text is opaque either way.

choices.text: Because the value is a string, and the server never read the JSON in it
choices.why: Right. `TYPE` said `string`; fields are something a hash has.

prompt: In a key-value design, how is "every order over 500 reais" usually answered?

choices.text: By a second structure written with each order and holding the answer
choices.why: Right: a sorted set of order ids scored by total, for example, kept in step with the orders.

choices.text: By a `GET` with a condition on the value, like a `WHERE` clause
choices.why: No Redis command takes a condition on a value.

choices.text: By an index the server builds on the totals as each order arrives
choices.why: The server does not know there is a total; it holds bytes.

choices.text: By asking for keys whose name matches `order:*` and a price
choices.why: A pattern matches key names, and the total is not in the name.

prompt: The shop wants Redis itself to keep a running sum of a customer's spending, exact to the cent. Which way of storing it does that?
hint: What type does Redis keep values in, and which command adds exactly?

choices.text: Text like "268.80", added with `HINCRBYFLOAT`
choices.why: That arithmetic is floating point, and a sum of many prices drifts away from the cents.

choices.text: Integer cents, like 26880, added with `HINCRBY`, which adds whole numbers exactly
choices.why: Right. Integer addition is exact, and the application divides by 100 to show it.

choices.text: A `Decimal128` field inside a hash
choices.why: That is MongoDB's type; Redis keeps every value as a string.

choices.text: A JSON string with the total inside, rewritten after each order
choices.why: Then the application does the sum, not Redis, and two writers can overwrite each other.

prompt: Which of these are true of a Redis hash, as the transcript showed it? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: One field can be read without reading the others
choices.why: Right: `HGET order:1001 total` returned the total alone.

choices.text: A field can hold another hash, so the order lines nest inside
choices.why: A hash is one level deep; the lines went in as JSON text.

choices.text: Every value comes back as a string, the total included
choices.why: Right: `"268.80"`, in quotes.

choices.text: The server can return every hash whose total is over 500
choices.why: There is still no query by value; the key is the only way in.

prompt: What does "wide column" describe in Cassandra?

choices.text: Rows grouped into partitions by a key and kept sorted inside each one
choices.why: Right. A partition of many rows is the "wide" in the name.

choices.text: Tables allowed to have thousands of columns
choices.why: The name suggests it; the model is about rows in partitions.

choices.text: Each column of a table in its own file, as analytics engines do
choices.why: That is column-oriented storage, a different idea.

choices.text: Columns wide enough to store whole JSON documents
choices.why: Width of a value has nothing to do with it.

prompt: With `PRIMARY KEY ((customer), ordered_at, sku)`, what decides which node holds a row?

choices.text: `ordered_at`, so that each day lands on its own node
choices.why: `ordered_at` is a clustering column: it orders rows inside the partition.

choices.text: The three columns, taken together as one key
choices.why: Together they make a row unique; only the part in the inner parentheses places it.

choices.text: `customer`, the partition key
choices.why: Right. Every row for one customer lives in the same partition, on the same nodes.

choices.text: `sku`, since products are spread evenly
choices.why: `sku` is the last clustering column; it orders lines within one date.

prompt: Ana's three rows came back with the August keyboard first, though the `SELECT` had no `ORDER BY`. Why?

choices.text: Because the keyboard row was inserted last
choices.why: Insertion order does not decide it; it was inserted third and came back first.

choices.text: Because rows are stored sorted by their clustering columns, ordered_at then sku
choices.why: Right. The order in the partition is the order on disk.

choices.text: Because cqlsh sorts every result alphabetically
choices.why: By SKU alphabetically, CB-012 would come before KB-101; it did not.

choices.text: By chance, since a single node returns rows in no particular order
choices.why: Inside a partition the order is defined, and lesson 3 relies on it.

prompt: A developer adds `ALLOW FILTERING` to the "lines over 500" query because it worked instantly in the lab. What happens on a cluster with millions of partitions?

choices.text: The same: the filter uses the clustering order
choices.why: `unit_price` is not a key column, so no order helps.

choices.text: Cassandra builds an index on first use and reuses it
choices.why: Nothing is built; every run scans.

choices.text: It scans every node to return a few rows
choices.why: Right. The usual fix is a second table whose partition key is the question.

choices.text: It is refused again, since the clause only works on one node
choices.why: It runs; that is the danger. The refusal was the warning.

prompt: Which of these questions is the sign that a graph store is the right tool?

choices.text: What was the total of all orders placed in September, across all customers?
choices.why: A sum over everything is a scan in any store, and a graph store is not the fast one at it.

choices.text: What did order 1001 contain?
choices.why: One aggregate by its id is a document or key-value read.

choices.text: What was the checkout's response time last Tuesday afternoon, minute by minute?
choices.why: Measurements over an interval are time series.

choices.text: How are these two accounts connected, through any number of shared cards?
choices.why: Right. A path of unknown length is what a graph store follows cheaply.

prompt: The checkout's response time is sampled every ten seconds on each of three servers. How many points does that add in one day?
What is TimescaleDB, as the lesson describes it?

choices.text: A metrics collector that asks each service for its numbers at an interval
choices.why: That describes Prometheus.

choices.text: A Postgres extension for time-partitioned data
choices.why: Right. Tables stay tables and SQL stays SQL.

choices.text: A graph database queried in Cypher
choices.why: That is Neo4j.

choices.text: A fork of Redis made after its 2024 licence change
choices.why: That is Valkey.

prompt: Put the life of one time-series point in order, from first to last.
items: Read at full resolution in recent ranges
trap: A point is almost never changed once written.

prompt: Match each question to the family built to answer it.
hint: One description fits none of them.

pairs.left: Give me the value filed under this name
Give me this whole order, lines and all
Give me this customer's rows, in date order
What is connected to this account, and through what?

prompt: A service records every sign-in of every account, and the only question ever asked is an account's last 50 sign-ins, newest first. Which shape fits best?
hint: Is it measurements to aggregate, or rows to fetch for one key?

choices.text: A time-series store, because every sign-in has a timestamp
choices.why: A timestamp alone does not make a time series: nothing is aggregated or downsampled, and the question is per account.

choices.text: A graph store, since accounts are linked to their sign-ins
choices.why: There is one hop and no path to follow.

choices.text: A wide-column table partitioned by account, clustered by time
choices.why: Right. One partition per account, rows already sorted; the question is one slice.

choices.text: A key-value store holding one string per account with every sign-in appended to it
choices.why: The value grows without bound and has to be read whole to find the last 50.
